To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the majority of children with GID do not persist with their gender dysphoria into adulthood, that the rate of persistence is higher in children who are more severely gender dysphoric in childhood, that the rate is higher in children with a strong cross-gender identity, that the rate may be higher in children with atypical gender development in other domains as well, and that the rate is lower in children whose parents are supportive of their gender dysphoric behavior.
(i) the persistence rate of gender dysphoria is high (around 80%) and (ii) the persistence rate is higher for boys than girls.

1) gender identity disorder in childhood is a rare condition, with a prevalence of 1.2 percent, 2) gender identity disorder is more common in boys than in girls, and 3) gender identity disorder appears to be stable over time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the factors that are associated with desistence or persistence of childhood gender identity disorder.
the development and maintenance of gender dysphoria and gender nonconformity, and how they relate to each other.
the development of gender identity in children and the factors associated with persistence and desistence of gender identity disorder.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the current evidence does not support the idea that gender identity disorder in children is a stable condition, and therefore, the current evidence does support a conservative approach of watchful waiting.
the evidence does not support a biological basis for gender identity.

gender dysphoria is a condition that is not only associated with significant distress and impairment in functioning, but is a condition which is also associated with significant morbidity and mortality.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found a significant relationship between gender dysphoria and sexual orientation in childhood, but not in adolescence.
gender nonconforming children are at increased risk for mental health difficulties.
we have demonstrated that the majority of young children who experience a gender dysphoria diagnosis will desist, and we have identified a number of factors that are associated with persistence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gender dysphoria is not a stable phenomenon, and that most children will desist from it.
the majority of children with gender dysphoria will not persist in their dysphoria.
gender identity is not fixed and that it changes over time.
